OPEN
This is open, and cannot be resolved with a finite computation.
For which $n$ are there $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$, no three on a line and no four on a circle, which determine $n-1$ distinct distances and so that (in some ordering of the distances) the $i$th distance occurs $i$ times?
#217: [Er83c][Er87b,p.167][Er97e]
geometry | 
distances
An example with $n=4$ is an isosceles triangle with the point in the centre. Erdős originally believed this was impossible for $n\geq 5$, but Pomerance constructed a set with $n=5$ (see [Er83c] for a description). 
Palásti [Pa87] constructed such a set with $n=7$. According to [Pa89] when Erdős saw this he asked whether there exists such a set of $5$ points with no equilateral triangles; Palásti [Pa89] constructed a set of $n=6$ points, satisfying these restrictions, with no equilateral triangles.
Palásti [Pa89b] has constructed a set with $n=8$.
Erdős believed this is impossible for all sufficiently large $n$. This would follow from $h(n)\geq n$ for sufficiently large $n$, where $h(n)$ is as in [98].

 Since many search attempts haven't yet found an $n=9$ configuration in general position that satisfies the problem requirements, I decided to see if configurations could be found if some of the requirements could be relaxed. That is, allow for a certain number of collinear triplets ($C$) and/or concyclic quadruples ($Q$). An AI agent was then asked to minimize $C+Q$ while ensuring multiplicities $1$ through $8$ in some order. As an aside, I believe some configurations exist in literature that maintain general position but relax the multiplicity restriction by simply requiring the sum to be $36$
The search returned an $n=9$ configuration with $(C, Q) = (1, 2)$ on a triangular lattice with lattice co-ordinates $P_0 = (4,-2)$, $P_1 = (4,-3)$, $P_2 = (2, 1)$, $P_3 = (3,-1)$, $P_4 = (2, 2)$, $P_5 = (-1, 0)$, $P_6 = (0, 0)$, $P_7 = (1,-1)$, $P_8= (3, 1)$. Squared distances for this relaxed configuration are $(1 ,3, 4, 7, 12, 13, 19, 21)$ which are the same as the Palasti configuration for $n= 8$ in general position with an additional distance $12$. The collinear triple is $\{P_1, P_2, P_3 \}$ and the concyclic quadruples are $\{P_0, P_2, P_3, P_4 \}$ and $\{P_4, P_6, P_7, P_8 \}$.
It is surprising (to me) that the bound is $C+Q \leq 3$, and I'm curious if it could be made sharper by lowering to $2$ or $1$ (which my agent has failed to do so far). For $n= 10$ the best it could do was $(C,Q) = (2, 2)$. Note that if 4 points are allowed to be collinear, this already brings $C =4$ by this definition.
Off-lattice configurations were also considered, and they were unsuccessful as well.

 A reference not yet on this page, and an extension of the computation in it.
Burt, Goldstein, Manski, Miller, Palsson and Suh, "Crescent Configurations" (arXiv:1509.07220), study exactly this question; their Definition 1.2 defines exactly the configurations asked for above, general position in the plane meaning no three collinear and no four concyclic. Their Remark 3.1 reports the only computational attack I can find: "With the help of a parallel computing cluster, we have exhaustively searched a 91 point hexagonal region of the triangular lattice for a construction for $n = 9$, but none exist. As the naive implementation took over 900 hours of computation for this size, better (and achievable) techniques are required to search a substantively larger region." Among their open problems is "Can planar constructions for $n \ge 9$ be found on the triangular lattice?"
I have extended that search. On the triangular lattice, squared distances are the integers $p^2+pq+q^2$, and collinearity and concyclicity are integer determinants, so the whole search is exact. Pinning one point at the origin and taking the rest at increasing indices makes it complete for every configuration whose squared diameter is at most $R^2$. The result:
no $9$-point crescent configuration exists on the triangular lattice with squared diameter at most $400$, that is, diameter at most $20$.
Their 91-point region is the $R^2 = 25$ rung of this ladder (the two point sets are identical, not merely the same size), so this reproduces their result in $2.7$ seconds and extends it by a factor of $16$ in point count and squared diameter, $91$ to $1{,}459$ points. The full ladder is about $3.1 \times 10^{12}$ search-tree nodes, $12$ hours on $5$ cores, zero solutions at every rung.
Two things keep this from being vacuous. The same program finds solutions at every $n$ from $4$ to $8$, and the first $n = 8$ solution it reports is Palásti's published configuration scaled by $\sqrt7$, with the identical multiplicity pattern. And the known constructions are small: on this lattice the tightest realisations have squared diameter $7$ at $n = 4,5$, $13$ at $n = 6,7$ and $21$ at $n = 8$. The $91$-point region covers squared diameter $25$, only $1.2$ times the $n = 8$ value; this ladder covers $400$, about $19$ times it. If a $9$-point configuration existed at the scale of every known smaller one, it would have turned up many times over.
One reading worth flagging: "in some ordering" is essential, and Palásti's own example shows why. Its squared distances $1,3,4,7,13,19,21$ carry multiplicities $1,4,5,6,7,2,3$, which is not monotone, so a search requiring multiplicity to grow with distance would reject the known example.
This says nothing about $n = 9$ in the plane. A crescent configuration need not have lattice coordinates, and larger-diameter lattice configurations are not excluded.
Code, run records, the exact verifier and a standalone audit (REPRODUCE.md):
https://github.com/sallerk/erdos-notes/tree/main/p217
Disclosure: the searches and computations were done with AI assistance.
